## The Weight Space View

Before moving to the full function space perspective, it helps to build intuition through a finite-dimensional parametric approach. The weight space view treats regression as inference over weight vectors, and the resulting structure naturally motivates the transition to Gaussian processes.

We begin with a linear model of the form
$$
f(\vx) = \vx^\top \vw,
$$ {#eq-linear-model}
where $\vw \in \R^D$ is a weight vector. To make this more general, consider an expansion of basis functions [@bishop_pattern_2006]
$$
f(\vx) = \sum_{j=1}^{M} w_j \phi_j(\vx) = \vphi(\vx)^\top \vw,
$$ {#eq-basis-expansion}

where $\vphi(\vx) = [\phi_1(\vx), \ldots, \phi_M(\vx)]^\top$ is a vector of basis functions mapping the input to an $M$-dimensional feature space, with weights $\vw = [w_1, \ldots, w_M]^\top$. This is more general than the simple linear model, allowing non-linear relationships through the choice of basis functions $\phi_j(\cdot)$, without breaking linearity in the parameters $\vw$.

Given training data $\mathcal{D}$, our goal is to learn the weights $\vw$. Maximum likelihood estimation would yield a single point estimate, but this ignores the fact that many different weight vectors could explain the observed data equally well yet make very different predictions elsewhere.

A Bayesian approach addresses this by placing a prior distribution over $\vw$, turning the problem into *Bayesian linear regression* [@bishop_pattern_2006; @gelman_bayesian_2013]. A natural choice is a zero-mean Gaussian prior:
$$
p(\vw) = \N(\vw \mid \vzero, \Sigma_p),
$$ {#eq-weight-prior}

where $\Sigma_p \in \R^{M \times M}$ is the prior covariance matrix. A common isotropic special case is $\Sigma_p = \sigma_w^2 \vI$, which gives i.i.d. Gaussian weights with variance $\sigma_w^2$ [@mackay_practical_1992].

Modelling each observation as $y_i = f(\vx_i) + \epsilon_i$ with independent noise $\epsilon_i \sim \N(0, \sigma_n^2)$, the likelihood for a single observation is
$$
p(y_i \mid \vx_i, \vw) = \N(y_i \mid \vphi(\vx_i)^\top \vw, \sigma_n^2).
$$ {#eq-likelihood}

Assuming independence across observations and conditioning on $\vw$, the joint likelihood over $\mathcal{D}$ is
$$
p(\vy \mid \vX, \vw) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \N(y_i \mid \vphi(\vx_i)^\top \vw, \sigma_n^2).
$$ {#eq-likelihood-product}

Collecting observations into the *design matrix* $\Phi \in \R^{n \times M}$ with $\Phi_{ij} = \phi_j(\vx_i)$ [@rasmussen_gaussian_2008] (see [Appendix @sec-design-matrix] for the explicit construction), @eq-likelihood-product compresses to a single multivariate Gaussian:
$$
p(\vy \mid \vX, \vw) = \N(\vy \mid \Phi \vw, \sigma_n^2 \vI).
$$ {#eq-joint-likelihood}

Applying Bayes' theorem:
$$
p(\vw \mid \vX, \vy) = \frac{p(\vy \mid \vX, \vw) p(\vw)}{p(\vy \mid \vX)}.
$$ {#eq-bayes-theorem}

Because the Gaussian prior is conjugate to the Gaussian likelihood, the posterior is also Gaussian [@bernardo_bayesian_2000]. Completing the square in the joint exponent (see [Appendix @sec-completing-the-square] for the full derivation) gives the posterior covariance
$$
\Sigma_w = \left(\sigma_n^{-2}\Phi^\top\Phi + \Sigma_p^{-1}\right)^{-1},
$$ {#eq-posterior-cov}

and posterior mean
$$
\bar{\vw} = \sigma_n^{-2} \Sigma_w \Phi^\top \vy.
$$ {#eq-posterior-mean}

The posterior distribution over the weights is therefore
$$
p(\vw \mid \vX, \vy) = \N(\vw \mid \bar{\vw}, \Sigma_w).
$$ {#eq-posterior-weights}

The observed data updates our prior beliefs about the weights to give this posterior, a foundational result of Bayesian linear regression [@bishop_pattern_2006; @murphy_machine_2013]. This posterior captures the uncertainty in the weights given the data, and allows for principled predictions that account for this uncertainty.
